being reflected.
When the Pharisee boasts of what he is and does, he is
not lying. He is in truth a pious man distinguished for his
piety and zeal, and in fact practises the works of piety which
he enumerates. Nor is it his real failing that he forgets that
there are also in his life, as in the lives of all men, things of
which he could not boast before man and God. His real
fault is rather that he should count up and boast of his good
works in the presence of God at all; in supposing that by
this means he can stand before God as "justified"
', i.e. that
God could not fail to deny him recognition and reward.
With his piety he does in truth serve God; but he serves Him
only in order to gain by this service recognition and reward.
By this attitude he discloses that what fills his being to its
depths is not love of God and goodness, but the need for
recompense. The more he exacts from himself in the way of
self-renunciation and sacrifice, the more passionate must be
his need for reward; the more proudly he points to what he
does, the keener is his sense of his own deserving.
But this means that the figure of the Pharisee does not
belong simply to a past age, and is not exclusive to the
Judaism of the period concerned or even to the Jewish
race in general, but is characteristic of humanity as a whole.
Modern psychology itself has taught us what a part is played
in every human life by the impulse to self-assertion. How
many of the words and deeds of men are attributable to the
desire to gain authority and importance, words and deeds in
respect of both good and ill, the moral and the immoral,
great achievements and great crimes. Psychology has shown
us how the natural need for recognition, if suppressed, can
assume morbid developments, and how a human life may
be ruined and brought to disaster if this desire for recog-
nition is repressed so that it results in a so-called inferiority
complex. For this reason great importance is attached in
education to helping the child to realize that it can achieve
something so that its consciousness of its own value may be
strengthened, and it does not need to feel itself to be inferior.
